newsitem.title: UK: BA Cargo sees major performance boost.
newsitem.headline: BA Cargo sees major performance boost.

text.p: The performance and quality of British Airways Plc cargo division will see major improvements by the time the airline's New World Cargo Centre(NWCC) at London-Heathrow opens in January 1999, Peter Read, general manager, new business said.

The greenfield 150 million sterling facility, now under construction, means "restructuring our business in its absolute totality...it will require different skills from today. No one will be in the business unless they have the proper skills and qualifications," he told a press briefing.
The airline's cargo operations, especially at Heathrow, have been criticised for its poor performance in recent years, industry sources added.

BA's cargo division has 2,900 staff worldwide with 1,500 at Heathrow. It has already announced that 400 current jobs will be lost when the new cargo centre opens, but it hopes to avoid any compulsory redundancies through voluntary severance, redeployment or early retirement.

Read added:" This week we have been in discussions with the unions on the changes. We're looking to simplify the grade structure to three -- operator, team leader and management -- grades. We're looking for flexibility across functions with new, lateral skills."

In addition to involving all its own worldwide staff, BA Cargo is talking to a number of its groundhandling agents to gauge their reaction to its Change Programme to improve perfomance and quality. In future overseas cargo handling will be through franchisees or BA Cargo's own dedicated operations, he said.
Apart from changes in the way staff work, BA Cargo said it is making a substantial commitment to improving the way freight is handled and processed.

"All freight and documents will be barcoded -- using the sophisticated International Air Transport Association (IATA) 6060 standard -- and tracked throughout its shipment period," said BA Change Programme executive, Matt Knox.
Extensive use will also be made of Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) to provide more information at the point of origin and to eliminate rekeying further down the processing chain, he added.

"Freight which does not conform to booking details will not be accepted, and there will also be random checks on some 20 percent of shipments to make sure they match up to the booked details," he said.

"The need for conformance is a critical part of the business as we have to know what to expect... this is no different from what Federal Express Corp, United Parcel Service of America and DHL Worldwide Express already require," he said.
"But customers who do conform -- by barcoding and making use of EDI -- will benefit from a "FastTrack" service, " Knox added.

The performance of the 200 outstations will also play an important role in ensuring the success of the new centre and if they do not meet or maintain standards:"he new building will not be effective." ((--Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44-171-542-7706 Fax +5017))
